$comment: REGISTERED MUTATIONS — the evidence behind every @regression test in tests/**.
WHY: two regression tests written during the 11.33.1 session passed with the bug fully
restored. They were vacuous, and only a hand-run mutation caught that. A regression test that
was never seen failing is a claim, not a check — so the claim is written down here in a form a
machine can re-run: `pnpm run check:mutations` applies each mutation, runs the specs that claim
to catch it, and REQUIRES them to go red.
Not part of `pnpm run check` (it deliberately breaks the source and re-runs suites; it belongs
in review and on the publish path, not in every inner loop). It is kept honest without running,
though: tests/unit/regression-evidence.spec.ts asserts that every `find` still matches its
target EXACTLY ONCE, so a mutation that has rotted into a silent no-op fails the normal suite.
id       referenced from the @seen-failing line of the tests it belongs to
file     path relative to the repository root
after    optional anchor; the search starts here (disambiguates identical lines in one file)
find     literal text, must occur exactly once in the search window
replace  what it becomes — the defect, reconstructed
specs    the spec files that MUST fail once the mutation is applied
driverSpecific  true when only some storage drivers are affected; `drivers` names them

mutations.defect: 11.36.0 — the exclude guard called `.test()` on the CONFIGURED RegExp. Projects declare `brevo.exclude` with the `g` flag (`/@(testuser\.com|test\.de)/gi`), and `RegExp.prototype.test` advances `lastIndex` on a `g`/`y` pattern, so one shared instance answered true, false, true, … for the same address. Every SECOND excluded recipient was therefore sent a real, billable transactional mail. Found in production: a CI e2e run delivered five mails to a `@testuser.com` address the project's own exclude pattern lists, and Brevo flagged the runner's IP rather than the project noticing.

11.35.0 — tightening the `_objectAlreadyCheckedForRestrictions` opt-out is the safe direction but NOT a silent one: a project that set the flag by hand loses its exemption and the fields it set the flag to preserve are stripped. Three customer projects do exactly that across twelve call sites. Without the one-time warning naming markRestrictionsChecked(), they would debug stripped fields with nothing pointing at the cause.

Not a shipped defect — a NEW feature, and this proves its wiring is not vacuous. `file.access` is only worth anything if CoreFileService.checkRights() actually consults the preset; a base implementation that still answered `true` would leave every preset a decoration, and every test that asserts a refusal would go green for the wrong reason.

Not a shipped defect — a NEW feature. The 'owner' / 'tenant' presets DECIDE on metadata.ownerId / metadata.tenantId, so the service has to STAMP them as it writes. Without that the preset is a rule about data that does not exist and every file becomes ADMIN-only — which is exactly the shape TUS uploads had before 11.35.0, and it was reported from downstream rather than caught by a test.

11.35.0 — the boot warning for an open file gate with no per-file policy fired only when multiTenancy was active. Too narrow: `downloadRoles: [S_USER]` with no rule leaks every file to every signed-in user whether or not tenants exist, and file ids are enumerable. The mutation restores the multiTenancy gate.

mutations.defect: 11.35.0 — CoreS3Service read ANY object as 'presigned downloads enabled', so the repo-wide `{ enabled: false }` pre-configuration idiom silently turned the feature ON. Reachable without TypeScript via NEST_SERVER_CONFIG / NSC__* JSON. The boot warning for this very feature DID honour the key, so the two paths disagreed and the disagreement resolved towards handing out session-less bearer URLs.

11.35.0 — the REFERENCE checkRights() (src/server/modules/file/file.service.ts, the shape every project copies) narrowed only 'id' and 'filename' and returned true for 'filterArgs'. A project surfacing findFileInfo() therefore exposed a full inventory of every upload — CoreFileInfo carries filename, length, uploadDate and the id, and for medical data the filename frequently IS the content. A yes/no hook cannot narrow a listing, so the rule must refuse the unrestricted one; a per-user listing is expressed by FORCING the filter server-side.

Not a shipped defect — this pins a gate that was correct but UNTESTED. `createFile()`'s own `checkInputType: 'file'` check was exercised by nothing: the canonical ownership rule the matrix installs returns true for every input type other than id/filename, so an upload refusal (quota, mime, tenant) was never verified to answer null or to leave no orphan bytes behind. The mutation removes the gate.

11.35.0 — the `_objectAlreadyCheckedForRestrictions` opt-out was a truthy test on a well-known property name, and nothing in src/ ever wrote it. So a document carrying `_objectAlreadyCheckedForRestrictions: true` (raw write, strict:false schema, restored export) disabled EVERY field-level @Restricted check for that object — silently, on the output path where a skipped check produces no error.

11.35.0 — every role guard resolved the request as `ctx.getContext()?.req || switchToHttp().getRequest()`, which yields nothing for a GraphQL subscription (the WS context has no `req`, and the HTTP fallback on a GraphQL context returns the resolver root). CoreTenantGuard then hit `if (!request) return true` and GRANTED access without deciding anything — and because the role guard delegates non-system roles to it when multi-tenancy is active, `@Roles()` on a subscription was checked by nobody: a plain `member` reached a tenantAdmin-gated subscription and received its messages.

11.35.0 — a finished tus upload's file metadata carried no owner, so the per-file ownership rule CoreFileService.checkRights() documents (metadata.ownerId === currentUser.id) could never authorize a tus-uploaded file: it failed closed for everyone but ADMIN.

11.35.0 — HEAD / PATCH / DELETE on a tus upload carried only the coarse tus.roles gate, so any authenticated caller who learned an upload id could read its offset, APPEND BYTES to somebody else's upload (whose content is then migrated into the file store under the victim's filename), or terminate it.

mutations.defect: 11.35.0 — a schema that DECLARES tenantId and is listed in multiTenancy.excludeSchemas lost its tenant filter with no signal anywhere. The framework's own docs carried `excludeSchemas: ['User', 'Session']` in a copyable @example, which on a project with per-tenant users switches isolation off for the user collection.

11.35.0 — checkRestricted() read restriction metadata off the VALUE's constructor only. An embedded subdocument read out of MongoDB is a plain object whose constructor is Object, which carries no @Restricted metadata, so every nested restriction evaluated to 'no restrictions' and the field was returned in full to callers who may not see it.

11.35.0 — GridFSHelper.findFileByName() read natural order (the OLDEST file of a reused name) while openDownloadStreamByName() defaults to revision -1 (the NEWEST). So getFileInfoByName()/getRawFileInfoByName() authorized against one document and getFileStreamByName()/getBufferByName()/duplicateByName() served another — an ownership rule approved the caller's own file and handed over somebody else's bytes.

11.33.0 — the S3 metadata lookups were gated on the ACTIVE driver instead of on whether S3 is usable, so adopting S3 kept GridFS readable while switching back turned every S3-stored file into a 404.

mutations.defect: 11.33.1 — GridFS keeps contentType inside `metadata` while s3-files / filesystem-files carry it at the document root, so findFileInfo() filtered on contentType matched every S3/filesystem file and NO GridFS file: nothing at all on the default driver, and every pre-switch file silently dropped on any other.

11.33.1 — writeFileFromStream() listened for errors on the DESTINATION stream only. pipe() does not forward source errors, so an aborted upload emitted an unhandled 'error' — an uncaught exception that ends the PROCESS. The same abort was a rejected promise under the S3 and filesystem drivers.

11.33.x — a COMPLETED tus upload's staged object is not an incomplete multipart, so no bucket lifecycle rule reclaims it. Without the explicit cleanup every finished upload leaves a full second copy of itself behind, in a bucket that by default IS the file bucket.

11.33.1 — CoreS3Service.putObject() handed a known-length body stream straight to the AWS SDK, which pipes it into its HTTP request without listening on the SOURCE. A failing body was therefore an unhandled 'error' event — an uncaught exception that ends the process. Reachable from tus finalization into S3, the one upload path that does not buffer first.

11.33.x — the Hub's Files panel read `fs.files` alone, so under `file.storage: 's3'` or 'filesystem' it reported 0 files and could not delete anything. In an operator cockpit a confident wrong answer is worse than an honest gap: it is the tool somebody opens BECAUSE they are unsure whether an upload landed.

mutations.defect: 11.34.0 — an S3-backed delete must REFUSE when CoreS3Service is unavailable. Deleting the metadata document while the object stays in the bucket produces an orphan nothing can find again — unrecoverable in a way that 'try again with S3 configured' is not.

11.34.0 — the Files panel merges three stores, so the union must be re-sorted before the page is cut. Without it the listing comes back GROUPED BY STORE, and `skip`/`limit` over that returns the wrong ROWS — the same defect sortMergedFileInfo() was fixed for, one layer up.

11.34.1 — MapAndValidatePipe built every message from constraintInstance.defaultMessage() alone, so a custom `message` in ValidationOptions (IsIn([...], { message: '...' })) was silently dropped and the client saw the generic default instead.

mutations.defect: 11.34.1 — only $property was substituted, so built-in default messages reached API clients with raw placeholders: "each value in roles must be one of the following values: $constraint1".

11.34.1 — the same custom-message gap existed on the non-customValidation path, which since class-validator 0.13 is reached by @IsDefined alone: its hardcoded message won over the message the developer wrote.

mutations.defect: 11.34.1 — the message renderer is a port of class-validator internals, and a port drifts silently: vendor-mode consumers resolve their OWN class-validator, so src/core/ can meet a version this repo never installed. Dropping $target is the smallest such drift, and no e2e case reaches that token — only the mirror invariant test does.

11.35.0 — CoreUserInput.roles had no content validator, so an admin could store a system role (s_*) in user.roles. hasRole() is a plain string intersection, so a stored 's_self' satisfied every S_SELF check on ARBITRARY users — update/delete of any account (mail/password change → takeover) without the account carrying a real role. Neutralizing the lookahead mutates the guard's DECISION rather than the existence of validation, so a red result is about this behaviour and not about the pipe having stopped running.

11.35.0 — the DTO validator only covers the input path. CoreUserService.setRoles() writes straight through findByIdAndUpdate, and force:true / bypassRoleGuard / direct Model writes never reach a pipe at all, so a system role could still be stored through any of them. Both remaining layers (setRoles' explicit check and the unconditional mongooseSystemRolePlugin) derive their decision from looksLikeSystemRole, so neutralizing it is what proves the non-DTO paths are actually guarded. NOTE: the two layers are DELIBERATELY redundant — mutating only setRoles' check leaves the plugin backstop in place and the specs stay green, which is the design working, not a gap. That is why the mutation targets the shared predicate rather than either call site.

11.35.0 — in tenant context the guard compared required roles against membership.role by plain string equality, so a member whose tenant role was literally 'admin' satisfied @Roles(RoleEnum.ADMIN), the GLOBAL platform role. Membership roles are customer-assigned free text (addMember takes any non-empty string), so any tenant owner could mint platform-wide access. Collapsing the global/tenant split restores it.

11.35.0 — checkRestricted passed the UNFILTERED required-roles list into checkRoleAccess, where a non-hierarchy role matches by exact string against the single available role. In tenant context that is membership.role, so a membership named literally 's_self' satisfied @Restricted(S_SELF) on ARBITRARY records — ownership was never compared. CoreTenantGuard already filtered system roles at its own call site; the decorator did not.

11.35.0 — the tenant plugin prepended $match to the SOURCE collection only. $lookup / $unionWith / $graphLookup read a DIFFERENT collection whose own aggregate hook never fires, so a single reporting-shaped aggregation returned every tenant's rows from the joined collection. For tenant-scoped medical data that is the difference between one tenant's records and everyone's.

11.35.0 — the tenant plugin stamped tenantId only when absent, and filtered WHERE but not the update payload. So a caller-supplied tenantId survived (planting a row in a foreign tenant) and an update could rewrite tenantId (moving a row out of its own tenant). Both are cross-tenant writes from an ordinary request.

11.32.4 §8 replaced multerFileFilter's bare-string rejection with `new Error(...)`, intending a clean 400. It never produced one: NestJS's `transformException` returns any NON-HttpException unchanged — its switch matches only multer's OWN message constants — so a file refused by the allow-list still reached the client as a 500, which tells the caller to retry a request that can never succeed. The test shipped with that fix asserted only that the callback receives an `Error`; it passed while the client got a 500, because it restated the implementation instead of the observable status.

mutations.defect: The same defect on the scriptable-type rejection path added by 11.32.4 §6 (`text/html`, `image/svg+xml`). Registered as its own mutation rather than folded into the allow-list one: that branch is the more security-relevant of the two, and a single mutation cannot show the other is covered — fixing one and leaving the other was the concrete risk here.

11.35.x — the §16 boot warning read CONFIGURATION only. `applyFileRoles()` writes onto the BASE-class member, but decorator metadata lives on the function object, so a subclass that RE-DECLARES a download handler keeps its own @Roles() and that is the function Nest registers. A subclassed getFileById() with @Roles(S_EVERYONE) therefore served anonymous downloads while resolveRoles('downloadRoles', …) still answered [ADMIN] and nothing fired — silence in exactly the deployment the warning exists for. Two independent consumer projects shipped it. This mutation re-introduces the blind spot at its narrowest point: the audit stops reading the handler's own metadata and sees only the inherited class-level roles.
mutations.find: const handlerRoles: string[] = Reflect.getMetadata('roles', fn as object) ?? [];

mutations.defect: Not a shipped defect — this proves the audit's WIRING is not vacuous. The subclass blind spot is only closed if DiscoveryService actually hands the initializer the registered file controller. If it returns nothing — provider never constructed, DiscoveryModule missing from CoreModule's imports, controllers absent from getControllers() for this application shape — every unit test still passes because they supply the classes through a stub, and the audit silently inspects nothing. A security check that quietly does not run is worse than none: its silence reads as a clean bill of health.

11.36.0 — the sign-in DTO carried @ApiProperty() only: documentation, no validation. Every line of the handler reads input.email, so a malformed body produced a TypeError and reached the client as a 500. On the most-probed endpoint any deployment has, that tells the caller to retry something that can never succeed and files their mistake in the same bucket as a real outage. This mutation strips the validators from the sign-in email so a present-but-wrong body is unguarded again.

11.36.0 — the OTHER half of the same defect, and the reason the validators alone are not enough. MapAndValidatePipe returns early on a falsy value (`if (!value || typeof value !== 'object' …) return value`), so a request with NO body is never validated: it reaches the handler as `undefined` and the first `input.email` read throws. Registered separately because each fix covers inputs the other cannot see, and a single mutation would not show that.

Not a shipped defect — a NEW option, and this proves its wiring is not vacuous. `revokeSessionsOnPasswordReset` is only worth anything if it reaches `instance.options.emailAndPassword`, where Better-Auth reads it on its three reset routes. A field that never arrives would leave a password reset silently keeping the attacker's sessions alive while the configuration says the opposite — worse than not offering the option, because the operator believes they took the precaution.

11.36.1 — `config.options` was merged over the resolved Better-Auth config with a SHALLOW spread (only `advanced` was deep-merged). An `options.emailAndPassword` therefore did not add a key, it REPLACED the whole block — including the `password: { hash: nativeScryptHash, verify: nativeScryptVerify }` pair the framework installs. Better-Auth silently fell back to its own hasher, so every credential already in the database stopped verifying and every user of that deployment was locked out at once, at runtime and with nothing in the logs. The module's own README recommended exactly that shape for wiring `sendResetPassword`.

11.36.1 — `src/templates/password-reset.ejs` was rewritten into a branded HTML mail that references `<%= appName %>`. The legacy caller `UserService.sendPasswordResetMail()` (and the byte-identical call in nest-server-starter) passes only `{ link, name }`, so `ejs.compile(tpl)(data)` threw `ReferenceError: appName is not defined`, `POST /users/password/reset-request` answered HTTP 500, and password recovery stopped working for every consumer that does not ship its own copy of the template. A template is never imported, type-checked or linted, so nothing else in the toolchain could see it.

With `cookies: { exposeTokenInBody: true }` the sign-in path converts the session token into a JWT for the response body (`resolveJwtToken`), which is what a bearer-using client needs. `processAuthResult()` then wrote that same JWT into the session cookie. Better-Auth resolves a session by the opaque token it stored, so the cookie pointed at nothing: the sign-in itself succeeded and every request afterwards was anonymous — `/iam/session` answered `success: false` for a session that plainly existed in the database, and a browser client was logged out again the moment it navigated. Invisible in the usual `local` baseline, where cookies-only mode makes the two values identical; it only bites in environments that set `exposeTokenInBody` (typically `e2e` / `ci`), which is exactly where nobody browses manually. Found from the outside: a consumer's whole Playwright suite passed locally (`lt dev test` runs NODE_ENV=local) and every authenticated spec failed in CI.

11.36.2 — the sign-in call site stopped handing the opaque session token to processCookies(), so with `cookies.exposeTokenInBody` the cookie was written from the body's JWT again. Better-Auth resolves a session by the opaque token it stored, so `/iam/session` answered `success: false` for a session that existed in the database and a browser client was anonymous on the next navigation. The sibling mutation `session-cookie-must-not-carry-body-jwt` cannot catch this: `processCookies()` returns early once a session token is present, so `processAuthResult()` and every unit test of it are unreachable from the repaired path. Reachable only in local/development/ci/e2e — assertCookiesProductionSafe() refuses exposeTokenInBody in production and staging.

SAFE_TEST_DB_PATTERN, the last guard before dropDatabase(), matched its markers as a substring ANYWHERE in the database name instead of as a delimited segment. `ci` hides inside soCIal / speCIal / finanCIal / priCIng / muniCIpal and `test` inside laTEST / conTEST / TESTimonials, so ordinary project databases read as disposable. tests/global-setup.ts drops whatever MONGODB_URI points at, and `lt dev up` exports it at the project's `<slug>-local` DEVELOPMENT database — so a developer on such a project who ran the e2e suite from that shell lost it, to the guard that exists to prevent exactly that. The guard had never had a test.

11.36.5 — RolesGuard returned early on a public endpoint (@Roles(S_EVERYONE), or no @Roles) BEFORE authenticating, leaving `request.user` unset. In a legacy-JWT deployment there is no CoreBetterAuthMiddleware on forRoutes('(.*)'), so the guard was the only thing that could identify the caller: a signed-in user arrived anonymous at @CurrentUser(), serviceOptions.currentUser and securityCheck(). A public endpoint that personalises for signed-in callers degraded silently, with no error and no log. Reported on an upgrade from 11.1.13, where the S_EVERYONE branch was evaluated AFTER the user had been resolved.

11.37.0 — better-auth 1.7 keys an account by (issuer, accountId) and sign-in filters on it verbatim (`account.issuer === createLocalAccountIssuer('credential')`). Every credential row written by 1.6 has no `issuer` field at all, so the comparison can never hold: the upgrade itself locked out EVERY existing password user, with a bare 401 and nothing in the log explaining it. The boot-time backfill closes that gap on the first start after the upgrade. Removing the call restores the lockout.

11.37.0 — the legacy->IAM account migration wrote the credential account WITHOUT an `issuer`, so better-auth 1.7 could not find the row it had just created. The very sign-in that triggered the migration answered 401, and every later sign-in did too. Dropping the field restores that.

11.37.0 — system setup linked the initial admin's credential account WITHOUT an `issuer`, so better-auth 1.7 could not resolve it. A fresh deployment created an admin who could never sign in — the one account that must work on a new installation.
